reception.text: The National Association of Audubon Societies' 1909 report claimed broad credit for the national bird reservations, though the Hawaiian reservation appears in its tables as a single line and none of its paid wardens worked in Hawaii.
reception.source: National Association of Audubon Societies, annual report for 1909

political_impact.text: The revenue cutter Thetis brought twenty-three poachers seized on Laysan and Lisianski into Honolulu, with about 259,000 bird wings and two and a quarter tons of loose feathers valued at $112,000.
political_impact.source: The Hawaiian Star, The Hawaiian Gazette and Pacific Commercial Advertiser (Honolulu), February 3–4, 1910

political_impact.text: A federal grand jury indicted Max Schlemmer, the Laysan guano-lease holder, but only under the immigration laws for bringing in Japanese workers; he was never charged over the birds.
The Biological Survey's later account put the raid at the plumage of more than a quarter of a million birds and dated it to January 1910; the Honolulu papers of the day give February 2.
political_impact.source: Henshaw, letter of transmittal, Biological Survey Bulletin 42 (1912), p. 3

legacy.text: The reservation became the Hawaiian Islands National Wildlife Refuge and later part of Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, among the largest protected areas on earth.
Papahānaumokuākea was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as a mixed natural and cultural site.

today.name: Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument
today.note: Established by Proclamation 8031, June 15, 2006; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2010.

later_actions.text: Included in Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, proclaimed under the Antiquities Act.

political_impact.text: The order put the bird preserves second to Reclamation Service use of the reservoirs, heading off any conflict with the water projects.

legacy.text: Most of the seventeen reservoir reservations were revoked between 1921 and 1968 as the reclamation projects and their uses changed; Deer Flat and Cold Springs were never revoked and remain national wildlife refuges.
Executive Order 7417 of 1936 misdates this order as February 5, 1909; it was signed February 25.

today.name: Minidoka Reservation

today.name: Carlsbad Reservation

related.note: Loch Katrine bird reservation, revoked by the same 1921 order that dropped East Park and four Washington sites.

reception.text: Bird-Lore claimed fifty-three national bird reservations in 1909, a total that counts the seventeen reservoir sites one by one.

political_impact.text: The orders passed with no floor fight, lawsuit or headline; Congress's unease over Roosevelt's public-land withdrawals never fixed on the small, scattered bird reservations.

legacy.text: Roosevelt established fifty-one federal bird reservations in all, counting the reservoir sites individually (thirty-five if Executive Order 1032 counts as one); they are the seed of the National Wildlife Refuge System.
